subtopic_detail: Positional pleuritic chest pain with widespread concave ST elevation and PR segment depression at thirty four
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 34 year old teacher with two days of sharp central chest pain that is worse when he lies flat and when he breathes in deeply, and that eases when he leans forward over the trolley. He had a head cold with a sore throat the week before.

He has no cardiac risk factors, takes no medication and has never used stimulant drugs. His pain does not radiate to the arm or jaw and is not associated with sweating or nausea. He has had no calf pain, no long haul travel and no recent surgery. A bedside echocardiogram performed by the emergency consultant shows normal ventricular function with no pericardial fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: A scratching sound heard at the left sternal edge in expiration with the patient leaning forward, no murmur, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no pulsus paradoxus, chest clear, calves soft
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows concave ST elevation in leads I, II, aVL and V2 to V6 with PR segment depression in those leads and PR elevation with ST depression in aVR, and no reciprocal ST depression; high sensitivity troponin 8 ng/L (less than 16) at presentation and at three hours; C reactive protein 34 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate transfer for primary percutaneous coronary intervention of the culprit vessel
options.rationale: The ST elevation is widespread across territories supplied by different vessels, is concave rather than convex, has no reciprocal depression and is accompanied by PR depression, none of which fits an occluded artery, and the serial troponins are normal. Activating the catheter laboratory here exposes a young man to an arterial procedure for a condition that is not ischaemic. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Start prednisolone 50 mg daily with a taper over four weeks and arrange review
options.rationale: Corticosteroid settles the pain quickly and is the intervention most strongly associated with recurrence, roughly doubling the chance of a further episode, so it is reserved for patients who cannot take anti-inflammatory drugs or who have an autoimmune cause. Early symptomatic relief is bought at the cost of a chronic relapsing course. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

options.text: Start high dose ibuprofen with colchicine for three months and restrict exertion
options.rationale: Positional pleuritic pain with a friction rub, widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and a raised C reactive protein after a viral illness is acute pericarditis, and the treatment is a high dose anti-inflammatory drug until symptoms and inflammatory markers settle, with colchicine added for three months because it roughly halves the risk of recurrence. Exercise restriction until the markers and the tracing normalise is part of the standard advice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

options.text: Start therapeutic low molecular weight heparin and arrange computed tomography
options.rationale: Pulmonary embolism causes pleuritic pain and must be considered, but he has no risk factors, no tachycardia, no hypoxia and no right heart strain pattern, and anticoagulation in a patient with pericardial inflammation raises the risk of haemorrhagic effusion and tamponade. The positional relief and the friction rub point away from it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

options.text: Start high dose ibuprofen alone for two weeks and arrange outpatient review
options.rationale: The anti-inflammatory component is correct and this is what was done for decades, but omitting colchicine forgoes the single intervention with randomised evidence of reducing recurrence, and around a quarter to a third of patients treated with an anti-inflammatory alone have a further episode. The difference from the correct answer is the second drug, not the first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

explanation.summary: Acute pericarditis is diagnosed when two of four features are present: characteristic positional pleuritic chest pain, a friction rub, widespread ST elevation with PR depression, and a new or worsening pericardial effusion. The tracing is the discriminator that most often decides the case in the emergency department, and the features separating it from occlusive infarction are the diffuse distribution crossing vascular territories, the concave morphology, PR segment depression with reciprocal PR elevation in aVR, and the absence of reciprocal ST depression. Most cases in Australia are viral or idiopathic and follow a respiratory or gastrointestinal illness, while tuberculosis, malignancy, uraemia, autoimmune disease and the post-cardiac injury syndromes account for the remainder. Treatment is a high dose non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug tapered once symptoms and C reactive protein settle, with colchicine for three months, and corticosteroid avoided because it predicts recurrence. Admission is warranted for the high risk features of fever above 38 degrees Celsius, subacute onset, a large effusion or tamponade, failure of anti-inflammatory treatment after a week, a raised troponin indicating myocardial involvement, immunosuppression, trauma or oral anticoagulant use.
key_points: Two of four diagnostic features are required: pain, rub, tracing changes, effusion
Widespread concave elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal depression separates it from infarction
Colchicine for three months halves the recurrence risk and is standard
Corticosteroid relieves symptoms quickly but roughly doubles recurrence
A raised troponin indicates myocardial involvement and warrants admission
explanation.pearls: PR segment elevation in aVR with PR depression everywhere else is close to specific for pericarditis and is the single fastest way to separate it from early repolarisation or occlusion on a crowded tracing, because it reflects atrial injury current rather than ventricular ischaemia.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Drowsiness with pH 7.28 after high concentration oxygen during transport for an exacerbation of airways disease
stem:
You are the emergency registrar receiving a 71 year old woman with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease who has had three days of increasing breathlessness with green sputum. The paramedics found her saturating at 84 per cent on room air and applied oxygen at 10 L per minute through a reservoir mask for the twenty five minute journey.

On arrival she is rousable but drowsy and cannot complete a sentence when she does speak. Her husband says she was talking normally when the ambulance arrived. She has had two admissions this year and uses home oxygen for sixteen hours a day. An arterial blood gas has been taken on the reservoir mask.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 142/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on 10 L per minute by reservoir mask, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable to voice, coarse tremor of the outstretched hands, widespread expiratory wheeze with poor air entry, no focal chest signs, warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Arterial pH 7.28 (7.35-7.45), arterial carbon dioxide tension 78 mmHg (35-45), arterial oxygen tension 145 mmHg (80-100), bicarbonate 34 mmol/L (22-32), chest radiograph shows hyperinflation with no consolidation or pneumothorax

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intubate her immediately and commence invasive mechanical ventilation in the department
options.rationale: Invasive ventilation is reserved for those who fail non-invasive support, cannot protect their airway, are haemodynamically unstable or are in respiratory arrest, and she is rousable with a maintained respiratory rate. Intubating a patient with this degree of airflow obstruction carries a difficult weaning course that is avoided whenever non-invasive measures can work. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide

options.text: Continue the current oxygen and start non-invasive ventilation immediately at the bedside
options.rationale: Non-invasive ventilation is the correct treatment for persisting respiratory acidosis and will very likely be needed, but delivering it while the inspired oxygen remains high leaves the driver of the hypercapnia in place, since the machine is entrained with whatever oxygen is supplied. The order of operations matters: titrate the oxygen first, then reassess. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide

options.text: Stop all oxygen therapy and reassess her arterial blood gases after twenty minutes
options.rationale: Removing oxygen entirely from a patient who was at 84 per cent on air twenty five minutes ago risks profound hypoxaemia, which kills faster than hypercapnia. The aim is controlled oxygen to a defined target range, not withdrawal. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute oxygen use)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute oxygen use

options.text: Give intravenous doxapram and reassess her arterial blood gases after twenty minutes
options.rationale: Respiratory stimulants were used before non-invasive ventilation was available and have been superseded because they cause agitation, arrhythmia and seizures while increasing the work of breathing in an already fatiguing patient. There is no current place for this drug in an Australian emergency department. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Titrate oxygen to a saturation of 88 to 92 per cent and repeat the gas in twenty minutes
options.rationale: A saturation of 99 per cent with a carbon dioxide tension of 78 mmHg after high concentration oxygen is the pattern of oxygen induced hypercapnia, driven mainly by worsened ventilation and perfusion matching and by the Haldane effect rather than by loss of hypoxic drive. Reducing the inspired oxygen to a target of 88 to 92 per cent using a Venturi device, alongside bronchodilators, corticosteroid and antibiotics, corrects the acidosis in many patients, and the repeat gas then decides whether non-invasive ventilation is required. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute oxygen use)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute oxygen use

explanation.summary: Oxygen induced hypercapnia is one of the few genuinely iatrogenic emergencies in acute medicine, and Australian ambulance and emergency protocols now specify a target saturation of 88 to 92 per cent for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure. The mechanism is largely a worsening of ventilation and perfusion matching as hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is released and blood is redirected to poorly ventilated lung, together with the Haldane effect, in which oxygenated haemoglobin carries less carbon dioxide; loss of hypoxic respiratory drive contributes much less than the textbook account suggests, which is why the respiratory rate may be near normal. A randomised Australian prehospital trial found that titrated oxygen roughly halved mortality compared with high flow oxygen in exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Management is controlled oxygen, repeated bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroid, antibiotics where the sputum is purulent, and a repeat gas at twenty to thirty minutes. Non-invasive ventilation is indicated if the pH remains below 7.35 with a carbon dioxide tension above 45 mmHg after that controlled oxygen and medical therapy, and it reduces intubation and mortality.
key_points: Target 88 to 92 per cent saturation in anyone at risk of hypercapnic failure
Ventilation and perfusion mismatch and the Haldane effect drive the rise, not lost drive
A near normal respiratory rate does not exclude oxygen induced hypercapnia
Repeat the gas twenty to thirty minutes after correcting the inspired oxygen
Non-invasive ventilation is indicated if pH stays below 7.35 despite that
explanation.pearls: A bicarbonate of 34 mmol/L tells you this is acute on chronic rather than purely acute retention, because metabolic compensation takes days to develop, and that distinction matters practically: her baseline carbon dioxide is chronically raised, so the treatment target is her usual state rather than a normal gas.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute oxygen use
Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide

subtopic_detail: Ferritin 140 with transferrin saturation 12 per cent in a man with heart failure limited by fatigue
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 68 year old retired carpenter in the heart failure clinic. His ejection fraction is 32 per cent and he is established on a beta blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, an angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor and a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor at target doses.

He has not been admitted for twelve months and is clinically euvolaemic today, with no rise in weight and no orthopnoea. What limits him is fatigue and breathlessness on the flat after about a hundred metres, which has not improved despite the last two dose increases. He has no rectal bleeding, no melaena and no dyspepsia, and gastroscopy and colonoscopy performed a year ago for a previous episode of anaemia were both normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 66 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure not elevated, no ankle oedema, chest clear, apex displaced, no hepatomegaly, no pallor of the conjunctivae
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (130-175), mean cell volume 88 fL (80-100), ferritin 140 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 12 per cent (16-45), C reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 110 micromol/L (60-110), faecal occult blood negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral ferrous sulfate daily and recheck his iron studies in three months
options.rationale: Oral iron has been tested directly in this population and failed to improve exercise capacity or repletion, because the inflammation of heart failure raises hepcidin and blocks intestinal absorption. The route is what fails here, not the decision to give iron. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

options.text: Give intravenous ferric carboxymaltose and recheck his iron studies in three months
options.rationale: In heart failure, iron deficiency is defined as ferritin below 100 micrograms/L, or ferritin between 100 and 299 with a transferrin saturation below 20 per cent, and he meets the second limb despite a ferritin inside the laboratory range. Intravenous repletion improves symptoms, quality of life and exercise capacity and reduces heart failure hospitalisation, and the benefit occurs whether or not the patient is anaemic. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

options.text: Transfuse two units of packed red cells and recheck his haemoglobin in three months
options.rationale: Transfusion is for symptomatic or severe anaemia, and his haemoglobin of 118 g/L is well above any transfusion threshold, while the volume load carries a real risk of decompensation in a failing ventricle. It also fails to replace the iron stores that are the actual problem. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

options.text: Start an erythropoiesis stimulating agent and recheck his haemoglobin in three months
options.rationale: Darbepoetin was tested in systolic heart failure with anaemia and did not improve outcomes while increasing thromboembolic events, so these agents are not used for this indication. They also cannot work without adequate iron available for erythropoiesis. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

options.text: Take no action as his ferritin is within the laboratory reference range for iron stores
options.rationale: Ferritin is an acute phase reactant and rises with the chronic inflammation of heart failure, so the standard lower limit of 30 micrograms/L does not apply and a value in the low to middle range with a low saturation indicates functional deficiency. Accepting the reference range at face value is the specific error this scenario tests. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is present in roughly half of patients with chronic heart failure and is an independent predictor of reduced exercise capacity, poorer quality of life and higher mortality, quite separately from anaemia. The reason ordinary reference ranges mislead is that ferritin behaves as an acute phase protein, so chronic inflammation raises it into the normal range while functional stores are exhausted, and transferrin saturation is therefore the more informative measurement. Heart failure guidelines accordingly use a disease specific definition: ferritin below 100 micrograms/L as absolute deficiency, or ferritin between 100 and 299 micrograms/L with saturation below 20 per cent as functional deficiency. Oral iron does not work in this setting because hepcidin driven by inflammation blocks duodenal absorption, so replacement is intravenous, typically as a single large dose infusion. Guidelines recommend screening for iron deficiency in all patients with new or worsening heart failure and repeating it periodically, and a newly identified deficiency still requires the usual thought about where the iron has gone, including gastrointestinal blood loss and aspirin or anticoagulant use.
key_points: Iron deficiency affects around half of heart failure patients and predicts worse outcomes
Ferritin rises as an acute phase reactant, so the usual lower limit does not apply
The heart failure definition adds ferritin 100 to 299 with saturation below 20 per cent
Oral iron fails because inflammation driven hepcidin blocks absorption
Benefit from intravenous repletion occurs with or without anaemia
explanation.pearls: Check his phosphate four weeks after the infusion: ferric carboxymaltose causes a fibroblast growth factor 23 mediated renal phosphate wasting that produces clinically significant hypophosphataemia in a substantial minority, and repeated infusions without checking have caused osteomalacia and fractures.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines
National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

subtopic_detail: A firm pink dome shaped nodule that has grown over eight weeks on the shoulder of a roof plumber
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62 year old roof plumber who has noticed a lump on his left shoulder that was not there when he started a job eight weeks ago. It now catches on his shirt and has bled twice.

It is 9 mm across, firm, dome shaped and uniformly pink with no brown or black in it. He has no other new or changing spots that he is aware of, and he checked against a photograph his wife took in January. He had a basal cell carcinoma excised from his back four years ago. On dermatoscopy there is no pigment network, and you see polymorphous vessels and milky red globular areas across the surface.

data_table.Examination: A 9 mm firm elevated pink nodule on the left shoulder with a small central crust, no surrounding pigment, no satellite lesions, no axillary or cervical lymphadenopathy, widespread solar keratoses over the forearms and scalp
data_table.Investigations: Dermatoscopy shows absent pigment network with polymorphous vessels and milky red areas, full blood count and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a punch biopsy of the centre of the lesion and review with the report
options.rationale: A partial sample can miss the deepest part of the tumour, and because prognosis and the width of the definitive excision both depend on the maximum depth measured in millimetres, an underestimate leads directly to an inadequate margin. Partial biopsy is acceptable only for very large lesions or cosmetically critical sites where complete removal is impractical. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma

options.text: Arrange a shave biopsy of the lesion and review the histology with the report
options.rationale: A shave removes the superficial portion and transects the base of a nodular lesion, which destroys the ability to measure depth accurately. It is a reasonable technique for a suspected basal cell carcinoma or a flat pigmented lesion, and a poor one for a raised nodule. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma

options.text: Apply liquid nitrogen cryotherapy and review the shoulder again in eight weeks
options.rationale: Cryotherapy destroys tissue without providing histology, so a melanoma treated this way is both inadequately removed and rendered impossible to stage. It is appropriate for solar keratoses, of which he has many, but not for a growing nodule. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists

options.text: Excise the whole lesion with a 2 mm margin down to subcutaneous fat for histology
options.rationale: A firm elevated lesion growing over weeks, with absent pigment network and polymorphous vessels on dermatoscopy, must be treated as a possible nodular melanoma, and complete excisional biopsy with a narrow 2 mm margin taken to the subcutaneous fat is the required technique because it preserves accurate measurement of the tumour depth. The definitive wider margin is then chosen once that depth is known. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma

options.text: Photograph the lesion for comparison and review the shoulder again in eight weeks
options.rationale: Short interval digital monitoring is a legitimate strategy for flat equivocal pigmented lesions, where change over three months distinguishes benign from malignant. It is explicitly not appropriate for a raised, firm, growing nodule, because this subtype grows vertically from the outset and gains depth during the observation period. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma

explanation.summary: Nodular melanoma accounts for around fifteen per cent of Australian melanomas but a disproportionate share of deaths, because it grows vertically from the beginning rather than spreading radially first, and because up to a third are amelanotic and therefore fail every element of the asymmetry, border, colour and diameter rule. The alternative rule for these lesions is elevated, firm and growing for more than a month, and any lesion meeting all three warrants excision regardless of colour or size. Dermatoscopy supports the suspicion when the pigment network is absent and there are polymorphous vessels and milky red areas. The correct diagnostic procedure is complete excisional biopsy with a 2 mm margin extending to subcutaneous fat, because Breslow thickness determines both prognosis and the width of the definitive re-excision, which ranges from 5 mm for in situ disease to 1 cm for tumours up to 1 mm thick and up to 2 cm for thicker lesions. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is discussed for tumours above 0.8 mm thick or with ulceration, primarily for staging and access to adjuvant therapy rather than for a proven survival benefit.
key_points: Up to a third of nodular melanomas are amelanotic and defeat the pigment based rule
Elevated, firm and growing for over a month is the rule that catches them
Complete excisional biopsy with a 2 mm margin to fat preserves depth measurement
Breslow thickness determines prognosis and the width of definitive re-excision
Short interval monitoring is for flat equivocal lesions, never for a growing nodule
explanation.pearls: Any firm pink nodule that has appeared and grown over weeks in an older Australian with heavy sun damage is excised rather than watched, because the median Breslow thickness of nodular melanoma at diagnosis is already above 2 mm and each additional month of observation adds measurable depth to a tumour whose prognosis is set by that number.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

subtopic_detail: Eighteen months of widespread pain with normal inflammatory markers and a proposed diagnostic steroid trial
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 55 year old childcare worker referred with eighteen months of pain in her neck, both shoulders, both hips, both hands and both feet. The referral asks whether a trial of prednisolone 15 mg daily would settle the question, on the basis that polymyalgia responds within forty eight hours.

She wakes unrefreshed however long she sleeps, describes her concentration as foggy, and has had alternating constipation and loose stools for years. Her stiffness is present all day rather than easing after the first hour, and it is no worse in the morning than the evening. She has no headache, no scalp tenderness, no jaw pain on chewing and no visual symptoms. There is tenderness over most muscle groups on light pressure, and no joint swelling anywhere.

data_table.Examination: Full range of movement at both shoulders and hips with pain reported throughout, no synovitis in any joint, tenderness on light palpation over the trapezius, gluteal and lateral epicondylar regions, normal power, temporal arteries non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 8 mm/h (less than 20), C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), creatine kinase 92 units/L (30-180), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), vitamin D 62 nmol/L (50-150), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the diagnosis and start graded exercise with sleep focused therapy
options.rationale: Widespread pain of more than three months with unrefreshing sleep, cognitive difficulty and associated functional bowel symptoms, in the presence of entirely normal inflammatory markers and no synovitis, is a central pain disorder diagnosed positively rather than by exclusion. Graded aerobic exercise and cognitive behavioural therapy directed at sleep and pain related distress have the best evidence, and a confident explanation of the mechanism is the intervention that makes the rest possible. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association

options.text: Start prednisolone 15 mg daily and reassess her pain after forty eight hours
options.rationale: The pattern does not fit polymyalgia rheumatica, which causes proximal shoulder and hip girdle pain with prolonged morning stiffness and a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C reactive protein in the great majority, and her markers are normal while her pain is distal as well as proximal. A partial response to steroid is common in any painful condition and would anchor her to a wrong diagnosis and years of exposure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology

options.text: Start prednisolone 15 mg daily and arrange temporal artery ultrasound as well
options.rationale: Investigating for large vessel vasculitis requires cranial symptoms such as new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual disturbance, or a raised inflammatory marker, and she has none of these. Imaging a normal artery to answer a question nobody has asked adds cost and a false positive risk. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association

options.text: Start a slow release opioid at night and reassess her pain in four weeks time
options.rationale: Opioids perform poorly in central pain disorders, and long term use is associated with worsening pain through hyperalgesia, along with dependence and cognitive effects that compound the symptoms she already has. Australian guidance advises specifically against them for this condition. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology

options.text: Refer for whole body magnetic resonance imaging to look for an inflammatory cause
options.rationale: Extensive imaging in the absence of objective abnormality reliably produces incidental findings that generate further tests and reinforce the belief that something has been missed, which worsens outcomes in this condition. The diagnosis is made on the clinical pattern with a limited blood panel. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association

explanation.summary: Fibromyalgia is a disorder of central pain processing, not a diagnosis of exclusion, and it is defined by widespread pain for at least three months together with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive symptoms, commonly with irritable bowel, headache and mood symptoms alongside. The most useful discriminators from an inflammatory rheumatic disease are stiffness that persists all day rather than easing after the first hour, tenderness on light pressure over muscle rather than joint line tenderness or swelling, and normal inflammatory markers. Polymyalgia rheumatica is the differential that most often leads to harm, because a partial response to corticosteroid is non-specific and, once a patient is on prednisolone, coming off it is difficult and the diagnostic label becomes fixed; true polymyalgia produces girdle pain with marked morning stiffness and raised markers in over ninety per cent. A limited investigation panel covering full blood count, inflammatory markers, creatine kinase, thyroid function and vitamin D is sufficient in the absence of localising features. Treatment is education, graded aerobic exercise, cognitive behavioural therapy and sleep management, with amitriptyline, duloxetine or pregabalin as adjuncts, and opioids and corticosteroids specifically avoided.
key_points: Diagnosed positively on the clinical pattern, not by excluding everything else
All day stiffness and light pressure muscle tenderness argue against inflammatory disease
Normal inflammatory markers make polymyalgia rheumatica very unlikely
Graded exercise, sleep focused therapy and education are first line
Opioids worsen central pain disorders and corticosteroids anchor a wrong diagnosis
explanation.pearls: A diagnostic trial of prednisolone is the trap to refuse: response to corticosteroid is not specific to polymyalgia rheumatica, patients with central pain disorders frequently report initial improvement, and the practical consequence is a patient on steroid for years with the adrenal suppression, bone loss and weight gain that go with it.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners
